# Style and Design: Scott Meyers
<!-- Slide 4 -->

## Style and Design: Scott Meyers

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images/myers.jpg){style="max-height: 55vh;" fig-alt="Scott Meyers"}
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
- Scott Meyers wrote *Effective C++*, design advice given as short, numbered items.
- His design philosophy: make interfaces easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly. If a mistake is possible, arrange for the compiler to catch it.
:::

::::

::: notes
Slides 5–9

A review of 11.02 before today's material. Hand out assets/Style_and_Design_-_Scott_Meyers.md. Students work in pairs for about 15 minutes, then discuss. The answer sheet is assets/Instructor_s_Answer_Sheet_-_Scott_Meyers.md.

The design philosophy is Meyers's Item 18, "Make interfaces easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly." Today's programs apply it to inheritance through Item 32: public inheritance means is-a, so everything true of the base class must be true of the derived class. Two programs model a penguin; both compile and run. Ask which one tells the truth.

The programs are illustrations inspired by Meyers's items, not code he wrote.
:::

<!-- Slide 5 -->

---

## Program 1

::: {style="font-size: 55%;"}
~~~cpp
class Bird {
private:
    string name;

public:
    Bird(const string& n) : name(n) { }
    string getName() const { return name; }

    void fly() const {
        cout << name << " flaps its wings and flies" << endl;
    }
};

class Penguin : public Bird {
public:
    Penguin(const string& n) : Bird(n) { }

    void swim() const {
        cout << getName() << " swims" << endl;
    }
};

int main() {
    Penguin pingu("Pingu");
    pingu.swim();
    pingu.fly();
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output:
Pingu swims
Pingu flaps its wings and flies

It compiles and runs, and it says something false. Penguin never mentions fly(), but inheriting from Bird brought it along.

Full program: cpp/meyers_program1.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 6 -->

---

## Program 2

::: {style="font-size: 50%;"}
~~~cpp
class Bird {
private:
    string name;

public:
    Bird(const string& n) : name(n) { }
    string getName() const { return name; }
};

class FlyingBird : public Bird {
public:
    FlyingBird(const string& n) : Bird(n) { }

    void fly() const {
        cout << getName() << " flaps its wings and flies" << endl;
    }
};

class Penguin : public Bird {
public:
    Penguin(const string& n) : Bird(n) { }

    void swim() const {
        cout << getName() << " swims" << endl;
    }
};

class Sparrow : public FlyingBird {
public:
    Sparrow(const string& n) : FlyingBird(n) { }
};

int main() {
    Penguin pingu("Pingu");
    Sparrow jack("Jack");
    pingu.swim();
    jack.fly();
    return 0;
}
~~~
:::

::: notes
Output:
Pingu swims
Jack flaps its wings and flies

Adding pingu.fly() does not compile: 'class Penguin' has no member named 'fly'. Bird makes no promise about flying, so the compiler rejects the impossible request.

Full program: cpp/meyers_program2.cpp
:::

<!-- Slide 7 -->

---

## Questions

::: {style="font-size: 80%;"}
1. In Program 1, list every member a `Penguin` has, and where each one came from.
2. Predict the output of each program. Do they match?
3. Is "A Penguin is a Bird" true in biology? Is it true in Program 1?
4. What happens if Program 2's `main` calls `pingu.fly()`? Is that better or worse than Program 1?
5. How does a `Penguin` give its name to the `Bird` part? In what order are the parts of `jack` built?
6. `name` is private. How does `swim()` print it?
7. A zoo adds an Ostrich, an Eagle, and a Duck that flies and swims. Which design do you extend, and how?
:::

::: notes
Short answers (the answer sheet has the full versions):
1. name (private, inaccessible), getName(), and fly() from Bird; the constructor and swim() from Penguin.
2. Program 1: Pingu swims / Pingu flaps its wings and flies. Program 2: Pingu swims / Jack flaps its wings and flies.
3. True in biology; false in Program 1, because Bird promises fly().
4. Compile error: 'class Penguin' has no member named 'fly'. Better: the compiler catches the mistake.
5. : Bird(n) in the initializer list. Bird, then FlyingBird, then Sparrow.
6. Through the inherited public getName(); private means this class only.
7. Extend Program 2: Eagle from FlyingBird, Ostrich from Bird. The Duck exposes the limit of the hierarchy and points toward multiple inheritance or has-a, later today.
:::

<!-- Slide 8 -->

---

## Discussion

- Should a class hierarchy model the real world, or the promises a program makes to the code that uses it?

::: notes
Ask which program students would rather maintain, then what is actually wrong with Program 1. Nothing is wrong with its C++; Bird makes a promise Penguin cannot keep.

Meyers's point: public inheritance is a promise. Bridge to Topic 1: overriding lets a derived class change how an inherited function behaves. An override that changes what the function promises is the penguin mistake in a new form, and Topic 1's Keep the Promise slide comes back to it.
:::
